summary: Defines a profile of TLS 1.2 that is fully compliant with the US government's NSA Suite B cryptography policy. It obsoletes RFC 5430. It is informational, its status is now historic, and RFC 8996 later updated it.

plainLanguage.summary: The government listed which secret-code tools were approved. This explains how to use only those in TLS, the lock on secure websites. It is old now and kept for history.

questions: what cipher suites does suite b tls use
which curves does suite b allow
subtitle: How to use TLS 1.2 while staying inside the NSA's Suite B cryptography rules.

tldr.problem: US national security applications must use only Suite B algorithms, and TLS offers many options that are not Suite B compliant.
tldr.mechanism: The profile restricts TLS 1.2 and DTLS 1.2 to two GCM cipher suites, two NIST curves (P-256 and P-384) and ECDSA signatures, at a 128-bit or 192-bit minimum level of security.
tldr.outcome: It is Informational, obsoletes RFC 5430, and is now Historic. RFC 8996 updated it.

today: RFC 6460 is now Historic. It obsoleted RFC 5430 and was later updated by RFC 8996.

sections.title: What the Profile Is
sections.content:
The United States government published guidelines for NSA Suite B Cryptography, which set the algorithm policy for national security applications. This document defines a profile of TLS version 1.2 (and DTLS 1.2) that is fully compliant with Suite B. It defines no new cipher suites. It picks from those already defined in RFC 5246, RFC 6347 and RFC 5289.

It obsoletes RFC 5430. The older transitional profile for TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1 and DTLS 1.0 moved to Annex A of this document.
sections.plainLanguage: There is an approved list of tools for keeping secrets. This document is the instruction sheet for using only those tools with secure web connections.

sections.title: Suite B Requirements and Security Levels
sections.content:
Suite B uses AES for encryption (key sizes of 128 and 256 bits), ECDSA for digital signatures and Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) for key exchange, with curves that have 256-bit and 384-bit prime moduli. The curves are P-256 (also called secp256r1) and P-384 (secp384r1).

Suite B defines two minimum levels of security, 128 and 192 bits. A system at the 128-bit level MUST use a cipher suite that fits Combination 1 or Combination 2 in full. A system at the 192-bit level MUST use Combination 2 in full. Suite B clients and servers MAY accept non-Suite B cipher suites for backward compatibility, but when two Suite B systems set up a TLS 1.2 session, Suite B algorithms MUST be used.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two strength settings, like a normal lock and a stronger lock. The stronger setting allows fewer choices.

sections.title: Cipher Suites, Curves and Signatures
sections.content:
Because GCM cipher suites are not supported before TLS 1.2, a Suite B TLS client or server MUST implement TLS 1.2 or later. A client at the 128-bit level MUST offer TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 or TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_256_GCM_SHA384, with the AES-128 suite preferred and listed first. At the 192-bit level the client MUST offer only the AES-256 suite. Any extra, non-Suite B suites must come after these in the ClientHello.

Connections MUST use secp256r1(23) or secp384r1(24), the first with AES-128 suites and the second with AES-256 suites. All authentication MUST use ECDSA: ECDSA-256 means P-256 with SHA-256, and ECDSA-384 means P-384 with SHA-384. At the 128-bit level either may be used, and one party can use ECDSA-256 while the other uses ECDSA-384. At the 192-bit level ECDSA-384 MUST be used. The client MUST always authenticate the server, while the server MAY authenticate the client.

Certificates MUST be ECDSA-signed and comply with the Suite B certificate profile in RFC 5759.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides must pick from a very short menu, and the strong setting has an even shorter menu. If the other side offers something not on the menu, a Suite B server will not choose it.

sections.title: TLS Extensions and Messages
sections.content:
A client that wants only Suite B generates a Supported Elliptic Curves extension containing just the allowed curves. At the 128-bit level it MUST include secp256r1 and SHOULD include secp384r1. At the 192-bit level it MUST include secp384r1. A server SHOULD check for the extension but MUST NOT choose a non-Suite B curve, even if the client offers one. If the client does not advertise an acceptable curve, the server MUST send a fatal handshake_failure alert and end the connection. Clients MUST check the chosen curve.

The client MUST include the signature_algorithms extension. Servers MUST include the matching ECDSA hash algorithms in the CertificateRequest message. The client signs CertificateVerify with ECDSA-256 or ECDSA-384, and the server signs its ServerKeyExchange message the same way, again with ECDSA-384 required at the 192-bit level.

Certification path validation MUST only accept ECDSA with SHA-256 or SHA-384. The RFC notes this is a change from RFC 5430.
sections.plainLanguage: During the handshake each side announces which approved tools it can use. The server only picks from the approved ones and hangs up if there is no match.

sections.title: The Transitional Profile in Annex A
sections.content:
For peers that cannot do TLS 1.2, Annex A keeps a transitional profile for TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1 and DTLS 1.0. It uses the Suite B algorithms as far as possible, with AES in CBC mode, ECDH on P-256 or P-384, the standard TLS PRF (with SHA-1 and MD5) and HMAC with SHA-1. The cipher suites are TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA and TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_256_CBC_SHA. The server MUST sign ServerKeyExchange with ECDSA and SHA-1.

The RFC states that this transitional profile is not a Suite B compliant implementation of TLS. It is a transitional path toward the compliant profile.
sections.plainLanguage: Some older devices cannot use the newest rules. This part is a stepping stone for them, but it does not fully meet the approved list.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Most security considerations are in the documents this profile builds on: the TLS 1.2 specification, the ECC cipher suites for TLS, and the AES GCM cipher suite documents (RFC 5246, RFC 4492, RFC 5288 and RFC 5289).

The one added point is consistency. Suite B TLS implementations MUST ONLY use the curves in Section 4.1. Otherwise the symmetric algorithms could end up much weaker or stronger than the asymmetric (elliptic curve) ones.
sections.plainLanguage: A chain is only as strong as its weakest link, so all the parts must match in strength.
